Tending a winter garden

Most of the plot sleeps from November to February, but a winter garden is not an empty one. Kale, leeks, parsnips and the last of the chard stand through the cold, and each of them asks for a little care: a cloche when the wind turns north, a mulch of straw over the roots, a path kept clear so the soil is not trodden into clay.

The frost does more good than harm. It sweetens the parsnips, breaks the clods that the autumn digging left, and kills off a share of the slugs that would otherwise wait for the first seedlings of spring. What it cannot do is help a plant that was sown too late, so the work of a winter garden begins in July, with the sowing calendar open on the shed bench.

On the shortest days there is little to do but look. That is worth doing too: the shape of the beds is easiest to judge when nothing hides it, and the notes made now, about what grew well and what did not, are the ones that decide next year's plan.

The Allotment, a newsletter for the plots on Mill Lane.
